subsubtopic: MR. OBERLE-CBC PROGRAM, "UP CANADA"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 8, 1974, the night before last, the government subsidized national television network aired a program called "Up Canada", a portion of which was dedicated to a soap opera called "One Honourable Member". It may be coincidental that this program was followed immediately by a program called, "Some Honourable Members". I, and I am sure most hon. members, appreciate the media's recognition of our presence here in Ottawa, but we must object to the use of the national network in creating a false impression about our activities here.
The scene in the opera showed one hon. member from the west coast, whose name and address were almost identical with those of one of my colleagues, in bed with another member's secretary. The male actor was clad only in a blanket with which he protected his vitals, and the female was devoid of any clothing apart from false eyelashes and fingernails.
An argument ensued in bed over the arrival of the member's wife from the west coast. The girl decided to "split the sheets" and she called a taxi which was to arrive in five minutes. As it happened, the taxi was on the spot almost immediately.
I would expect, Mr. Speaker, that the minister responsible for financing the corporation would make every effort to stop the continuation of this exhilarating cultural experience so that we do not create the impression in Canada that any member or his secretary can call a taxi in Ottawa and expect to have it arrive in less than half an hour.

subsubtopic: MR. OBERLE-CBC PROGRAM, "UP CANADA"
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to establish a study committee to examine the feasibility of a political or economic union with the Crown colony of the Caribbean Turks and Caicos Islands following upon a visit of Canadian parliamentarians to the islands as a result of an invitation by the state council of the islands.
The elected members of the state council consider that one solution to the needs of the islands is Canadian association. They would like to investigate seriously the possibility of these islands becoming an overseas maritime province or territory of Canada.

He said: Hon. members will appreciate that I rise once again to speak on this bill with some regret, even though I repeat how important a measure it is. Like many hon. members, I had hoped this House had disposed of the matter and that it would be on its way to becoming the law of the land. This is an important bill. There are many clauses in it which should not be lost sight of, even though we are dealing with some rather different and special areas. It is important because it makes it an offence to intrude upon individuals in this country or to possess electronic intrusion devices.
When we disposed of this bill last, we had a debate in this House on the particular clause which is now in issue, the clause which was deleted in the other place. Rather than allow it to be deleted, I propose in my motion to substitute therefor a different form of words. When this specific notice provision was before the House last, I indicated my doubt about the real importance or desirability of having that provision, having regard to the fact that we are dealing here only in the area of wiretaps which are legal in their nature and which are authorized. It is only in that case the notice provision comes into play and requires some further examination from time to time by a judge as well as notice concerning those authorizations which have been given.
I also indicated to the House something which concerned me about the clause, and which in later discussion also concerned members in the other place. I refer to the fact that the clause, as originally proposed by the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey), seemed to be rigid in the sense that it required, in certain circumstances, notice to be given of criminal investigations when those investigations were not complete which might, therefore, seriously interrupt and interfere with those investigations.
There has been some discussion of this subject in the press. I read it again in this morning's Globe and Mail. It is to the effect that one can go back to a judge again and again under the clause as proposed by the hon. member for St. Paul's. That is not so. That is not how the clause reads. The clause basically requires notice of an intrusion by the police under a lawful authorization, that notice to be given within a 90 day period following the authorization. There is an exception to that which would allow the going back to a judge, but really only within the 90 days. The words of the clause require the attorney general to certify within the said 90 days that the investigation was continuing. In that case, an exception could have been granted by a judge.
When speaking before the Senate committee, the police indicated that in one particular famous example, the Zizzo case, they were sure this would have interfered with the investigation to completion of a very serious offence. The Zizzo case was the subject of court proceedings in Toronto in 1973. Heroin importation of a very serious nature was involved. The conviction of the persons who were involved led to certain life sentences being imposed. Therefore, we are dealing with no light matter: the importation of heroin into Canada which led to life sentences. In that case the police investigation included the use of certain electronic intrusion devices spread over a period beginning in May
Protection of Privacy
1971 and not completed until 1973. If in that period of time the police had had to give notice after 90 days, they are sure that would have been the end of their opportunity to apprehend these criminals. This is a very serious matter, indeed.
It also appeared to the committee looking at this question that a judge might have granted a certain extension. However, there is some real question whether he would grant an extension of one or two years on the one occasion he could grant an extension under the clause in question. It was this point which troubled me originally, which troubled the members in the other place, and which led them to delete the section. In the other place, appearing before members there, I did attempt to urge them to pass the bill as it stood rather than see this important piece of legislation fail to become law. I urged upon them the possibility of our watching the section and introducing amendments in short order, if necessary, to cover any deficiencies rather than hold up the bill. I did this recognizing the procedural difficulties in which we could get ourselves if we did not find a compromise.

I think the hon. members in the other place were somewhat impressed by the fact that the decision on this issue in the House had been very close-that we had decided by a vote of only 118 to 113. This, too, may have influenced their course of conduct. As a result, we were presented with the choice of either concurring in what the Senate had done, which, as hon. members will realise is what I had originally suggested, or sending the bill back to them in its original form. Another option would be to continue some of the work upon which we had been engaged, that is to say, endeavour to reach a compromise which could rescue us from a difficulty and produce a reasonable solution. Such a compromise would be one which met the wishes, to a large extent, of members like the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey) who felt that notice was desirable and even though I could not see the particular merit of that position, I was willing to put such a compromise before the House in the motion we are now considering.
Discussions have been held with members opposite, and I acknowledge the contribution of some words in the motion itself by the hon. member for St. Paul's, particularly the reference in subsection (1) and elsewhere to the interests of privacy. In subsection (2) the hon. member requested that the words "and in the interests of privacy" be added to the words I had proposed, "in the interests of justice". I was willing to go along with that suggestion, although I felt the existing wording was sufficient. It was clear there was agreement to attempt to pass a motion of that sort, putting a new notice-provision in the bill, and to return it to the Senate in that form in the hope that it would overcome the objection raised by their Honours and thus allow this important piece of legislation to become law.
What I now urge upon hon. members is that above all we should allow this matter to be decided quickly in the House; that we not be carried away by subsidiary or other points. I make this plea particularly to those hon. members who are interested in opportunities to speak about the other place in a variety of ways. In my view, this is not the time to do so. This is an important piece of legislation and

If that is the Minister of Justice's idea of a question of privilege, it is no wonder that this bill is in trouble. I am sorry that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is not here, but I want to say that it is not good enough for the Prime Minister to shrug off his responsibilities with the remark that some bills are always left on the order paper at the end of a session.
This bill is not just another bill. It can in no way be dismissed under the general category of "some bills which die at the end of a session". The protection of privacy bill is at least the fourth piece of such legislation to be considered by parliament. A bill on the same subject was given first reading on June 28, 1971; it died at the end of that session in February, 1972. Another effort was made on February 21, 1972; this bill was considered by the same committee and reported back to the House on June 14 of that year with amendments. Once again events intervened and the bill died on the order paper.
That does not end the chronology, for a private member's bill was introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) back in 1969 or thereabouts. The Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs reported that bill on March 11, 1970, but no further action was taken by the government and the bill died when the session ended in October of that year. In light of all that time and effort expended by parliament and its committees, surely it would be irresponsible for the government to let it all go by default. This is why we in this party are prepared to stay here to see this bill through its final stages.
The Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, in its unanimous report of March 1970, recommended that a provision respecting notification be included in any legislation to protect privacy. When the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey) spoke on this bill on second reading on March 7, 1973 he urged the minister to include a mechanism for notifying a citizen that his privacy had been invaded. During the consideration of the bill by the standing committee, the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) again urged the minister to have his officials prepare an amendment covering notification. When the minister failed to respond to these urgings, the hon. member for St. Paul's moved an amendment which was adopted by the standing committee and subsequently by the House. I thought that this sequence of events, this little chronological story, was important since some have claimed that the action of the standing committee and the House regarding notification was hasty and ill-considered. Nothing could be further from the truth.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The amendment proposed by the minister once again involves an important principle, a principle similar to that on which the House has just divided. It concerns the power of the Senate to thwart the bill of the elected representatives of this parliament. I urge the House to reaffirm the position it took a few minutes ago by rejecting the amendment put forward by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
The emergency allocation bill is designed to deal with the situation in the event of a shortage of oil products in this country. A board will examine the situation and the government will declare a national emergency if it is thought that is necessary. This House would then debate the issue and could, by a negative vote, rescind the declaration of emergency. However, if this House were to affirm that there was indeed an emergency, and that government allocation of fuel supplies was necessary to protect Canadians, then if this amendment were passed the Senate could negative the motion and thwart the will of this House. I say that such a situation is completely intolerable. If Canadians anywhere in Canada are short of fuel, are cold in their homes, if schools cannot open, if hospitals must go without fuel and if workers must be laid off from their factories because the Senate has reversed a decision of this House, then what has happened to our parliamentary democracy?
As we all know, members of the Senate are not elected by the people whom this bill is designed to protect, they are appointed. It is often the case that the other place is a repository for political has-beens. We should remember also that many members of the Senate are on the boards of directors of multinational oil companies, and other companies connected with energy supply in this country. How can we expect them to have an unbiased view of the energy situation? I can see no way that the members of this House can tolerate a privileged, appointed group being given the power of veto over this very important piece of legislation.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) pointed out yesterday that when we in this country had an emergency of another sort and we invoked

the War Measures Act, the other place was not invited to pass on the resolution. It was the House of Commons, the elected representatives of the people, who made that decision. I submit that a national emergency which affects the lifeblood of this nation economically, as well as the wellbeing of all Canadians, should also be dealt with in this House and not in the other place.
I urge the members of the Conservative party, who today voted with the NDP in a sense to reject a Senate veto, the negativing of a motion passed by this House, also to vote against the government's amendment. If we reject the amendment we are not taking power away from the Senate, because the Senate does not have this power to begin with. But if we pass the amendment we will be giving the Senate the power of veto, which in my opinion would create a very dangerous precedent.
There are many precedents in the British North America Act for not requiring the Senate to make a decision on legislation or motions that are passed by this House. Under section 91, I believe it is, if war breaks out this House can make a decision to sit beyond the normal five-year tenure of parliament without reference to the other place. We are the elected representatives of the people and are concerned to protect those we represent. This is why we must retain the long honoured principle that it is the elected representatives of parliament who make the crucial decisions on national matters, and that such decision should not be placed in the hands of the appointed, non-responsible members whom we find in the other place. I am sure that, upon reflection, members of the Conservative party will agree that this is a dangerous power to give to the Senate. As I say, in light of our political duties and our duties to our constituents, the House of Commons should be the place where the decision is made. I urge members of the Conservative party to reject the minister's amendment which would give this power to the other place.

First of all, may I deal with the comments made yesterday by the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais), who has a very good, trained voice, such a trained voice that he sat in his place in the committee, and when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) just raised his eyebrows, the hon. member for Nipissing was on his feet to move amendments. It was a great example of ESP. Indeed, I thought the hon. member was in training to be a parliamentary secretary; on his performance in the standing committee he certainly earned it.
The hon. member made a comment about the multinational oil corporations, and how this party might have changed its position. We will give the hon. member a chance to test his relationships with the multinational corporations, as well as my hon. friends to my left, in a little while with another amendment. But let me tell the hon. member that when the members of this party in committee saw, as a result of honest, hard-working negotiations that took place prior to the Christmas recess, that the government was prepared to accept an amendment to the bill that would make parliamentary approval a condition precedent to the government's declaration of an emergency, and that the minister indicated there would be a parliamentary right to review, and if necessary to revoke, that declaration of emergency, then and only then did this party make a change in its position.
It was our opinion, as we so stated during the course of second reading, that without that safeguard this was not the kind of power that should be placed in the hands of the government. This has nothing to do with the multinationals. As a matter fact, we disapproved of the position taken by the multinational corporations, as expressed by the official from Exxon or Imperial Oil who appeared before the committee. He said that he loved the bill, that he was delighted with it. Of course he would be, because one of the effects of the bill would be to give the multinational oil companies legal sanction to do what they have been doing all along, that is to arrange a form of allocation of supplies which has suited them not only domestically but externally. Indeed, I read that there is now being carried on in the United States a close examination and scrutiny of precisely the position taken by some of the multinational oil corporations regarding exaggerating the energy crisis.
I was not privy to what went on in the discussions of the technical advisory committee, but I would consider it very likely that this bill has its genesis in the technical advisory committee. The representatives of the large oil companies said they loved it and welcomed it. As the president of Imperial Oil said before the committee, they would like it a little better if they were given blanket exemption from the provisions of the combines legislation. They would like a measure whereby they could get a better form of compensation, but they said outside of that the bill was fine. Of course it is fine, because it is just giving them legal approval to continue doing what they have been doing and wanted to do. subsubtopic: PROPOSED MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-REQUEST FOR COPY OF TRAINING AND EMPLOYMENT AGREEMENTS PREPARED BY INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
He said: Mr. Speaker, some months ago I placed a motion on the order paper. I had hoped that it could have been debated before this time, but I realize a large number of motions precede it and that other members of the House have problems which they feel they would like to have debated in this assembly. The following is my motion:
That an Order of the House do issue for a copy of training and employment agreements prepared for the proposed Mackenzie Valley pipeline as referred to at page 61 of the Annual Report of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
We have had difficulty in obtaining studies and information from the government on programs related to a potential Mackenzie Valley pipeline. We are told action is being taken in this field by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, but to date very little information has been made public by the department. This House has a right to know what specific steps have been taken, and what reports have been made regarding the training and employment plans for northern people once the Mackenzie Valley pipeline gets underway.
I should like to refer the House to the 1971-72 Annual Report of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. It deals with this matter at page 61 and states:
A special staff group in the Department has been charged with the task of seeking effective means to increase employment and provide greater economic opportunity for northern people.
The pipeline industry and associated trade unions have contributed material and information to enable the Department to prepare a training and employment agreement for the proposed Mackenzie Valley pipeline. Industry and other government departments have suggested areas of training having potential for permanent employment.
My motion is designed to obtain specific information from the government concerning the progress made in its plans, as announced almost two years ago, to prepare a training and employment agreement for the proposed Mackenzie Valley pipeline to ensure greater economic opportunity for the northern people. I have several questions which I hope will be answered this afternoon.
First, has a training and employment agreement to assist northern people been formulated by the department, and if so what is it? If no plan has been prepared to date, is one in the making and when will it be ready? If no training and employment agreement will be produced by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, then what is being done to carry out the policy announced in the 1971-72 annual report?
I feel there is some urgency to this matter. There have been frequent statements from various cabinet ministers suggesting an early start on the Mackenzie Valley gas line. We have heard from the potential pipeline builders that an application could be made at an early date, perhaps within the next few months. There is no doubt that it would take at least a year before any application could be approved. Nevertheless, any effective type of training and employment agreement must be in effect at an early date if we are to have a genuine effort to provide greater economic opportunity for our northern people when these projects are underway.
Personally, I see no reason for the early building of a Mackenzie Valley gas line. It should be built to provide
Mackenzie Valley Pipeline
energy cheaply for the Canadian market and not overwhelmingly for export, as the present plans of the gas and oil companies indicate. We have had enough sell-outs of our non-renewable oil and gas resources. I hope a new approach to the development and use of these energy resources will develop in time to conserve much of these valuable resources for future Canadian use. Despite this position, we feel that the training programs and employment agreements to assist in improved economic opportunity for the northern people must go forward. They must deal not only with pipeline construction but with a number of potential economic and other developments in the north.
There are other reports on pipeline development which should be made public as soon as possible. All this information is essential if we are to be able to make those decisions which are in the best interest of Canada. It is not my intention to prolong my remarks on this matter, but I again point out that there are a host of problems facing us in the north. They deal with native rights, environmental protection, the wise use of resources and so on. Our NDP group insists that it have all the information for discussion on these matters so that they can be resolved in a proper manner and at an early date.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: PROPOSED MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-REQUEST FOR COPY OF TRAINING AND EMPLOYMENT AGREEMENTS PREPARED BY INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding) has brought this matter to the attention of the House at this time. Regrettably, we do not have the particular information to provide the hon. member at this time. Also, he asks some specific questions. I want to tell him that the department is still in the process of preparing such an agreement. It is still in draft form, and is continually being revised to reflect technological change related to both the construction and operation of gas transmission lines. It will take into account also the social and economic impact of such a major project in the Mackenzie Valley.
In this regard, the agreement is being prepared to ensure the maximum employment of northern residents during the construction and operation of the pipeline, should it go ahead. Also, the agreement will stress permanent positions for northern residents in the employment which the pipeline will create, such as in the operation of the pipeline, increased exploration activity, gas field development and operations related to petroleum activity. This is consistent with the government policy for northern development for the 70's which stated that the native people should derive early and tangible benefits from the economic development, and be seen to benefit. It will be remembered that in August, 1970 the government announced the initial guidelines for the construction and operation of northern pipelines.
Mr. Speaker, in order to let the House and the hon. member for Kootenay West know how serious we are that the best possible situation be created in respect of employment for the native people, and for the general residents of northern Canada, I should like to go over some of the guidelines, the expanded guidelines, made public on June 28, 1973 by the minister. We are very keen about this. We want to make sure that the native people and all northerners benefit to the maximum from the creation of the pipeline which perhaps will eventually go through the north. I shall go over some of these guidelines briefly in

January 10, 1974
Mackenzie Valley Pipeline
order to indicate the kind of things we are very concerned about.
I will read some of these guidelines:
1.	The Applicant must undertake specific programs leading to the employment, at all occupational levels, of residents of the territories- and in particular native people, during the construction and operation of the pipeline. Such programs or projects shall include but not be limited to: advance information on all jobs in a manner that ensures that the information reaches potential workers; skills required for various occupations and anticipated duration of employment; upgrading and skill training; other forms of integrated training that include on-the-job work experience; and counselling for those unfamiliar with industrial jobs or wage style living-
2.	Priority placement in jobs shall be accorded native people of the territories in keeping with the tenor of Article 5 of the International Labour Organization Convention, 111, 1958, ratified by Canada, and the government's intent to increase employment opportunities for members of disadvantaged minority groups. During the consultation between government, unions and employers as outlined in the Convention, ways and means will be found to ensure access for these employees into the appropriate union locals and hiring halls where there is a requirement. In addition, in accordance with the principle of employment of local workers which is accepted by organized labour, the applicant will employ labour from the locality where work is being executed to the extent it is available. The applicant shall comply with the above Convention and employment principles, and co-operate with government's effort to operate an effective recruitment, placement and counselling service.
3.	The collective agreements signed by the applicant and organized labour shall not distinguish between residents of the territories and others respecting special benefits and allowances, including housing for operational staff, and the nature of these benefits shall be in no way inferior for employees from the territories.
These are just some of the brief indications in the guidelines. Guideline no. 4 reads:
4.	Contracts and subcontracts shall be so designed and publicised as to invite and encourage bids from native organizations, settlement councils and local contractors. In addition, the businesses and commercial organizations of the territories shall be invited and encouraged to supply goods and services required for thf pipeline development and operation.
5.	A substantial number of native people depend on trapping and hunting as a principal means of livelihood, and many derive a real satisfaction from being on the land and being master of a familiar environment. Therefore, the pipeline will be constructed, operated and abandoned with minimal interference to traditional trapping, hunting and fishing areas. In addition, where the pipeline construction is planned to be located in proximity to a settlement-particularly a native settlement or localized area subject to intensive use, then the location of construction camps, associated activities and the detailed siting of the pipeline will be decided by government after consultation with the applicant, and the settlement council, or local government body, or the native organization.
I do not want to read further from these guidelines, but I would be happy to provide a copy of them to the hon. member if he wishes.
As I said before, the minister has already made these public. I want to assure the hon. member that once the agreements are signed, it is our intention to make them public so that everyone will know what our intentions are. We are looking at this matter of possible pipeline construction in the north-there has been no application so far-with the greatest of seriousness, and we want to make very sure that the mode of life of the people in the north will not be disrupted in any major way. We want to ensure that the native people and the northern residents will gain the maximum benefit from any pipeline, both

during the construction stage and later in the operational stage.
I know that there are other hon. members who wish to participate in this debate, and therefore I will end my remarks at this point.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subsubtopic: PROPOSED MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-REQUEST FOR COPY OF TRAINING AND EMPLOYMENT AGREEMENTS PREPARED BY INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words about employment for northerners from the viewpoint of the Department of Manpower and Immigration. I do not think it is necessary to outline to the House what the responsibilities of the department in general are. I think they are sufficiently well known, but the extent to which these services are being provided in the Northwest Territories may not be realized. The services of the department in that area are extended not only to the major population centres but also to people in more remote areas, especially through provision of itinerant services.
The department determines the manpower needs of employers in the north and arranges for suitable training courses for northern residents so that their job qualifications might be acceptable to these employers, and in assessing this and all other questions involving manpower in the north it follows the advice of the manpower needs committees. As the House is probably aware, these committees have been set up in all provinces and are composed of representatives of provincial governments and the federal government. In the territories, it is the territorial government which is represented along with the department. It is this committee that is able to bring both national and local expertise to bear on analysing manpower needs. Its advice is followed with respect to the particular problems which arise.
Full time offices of the department exist in Yellowknife and Inuvik, in the western Arctic region, and there are two branch offices at Hay River and Fort Simpson. In addition, there is the main training centre at Fort Smith. During 1973, a full time centre was opened at Frobisher Bay to provide regular service to Baffin Island and the high Arctic area, and itinerant services are also provided from this centre so that there is complete coverage, as complete as possible, of this vast area.
The branch office in Fort Simpson opened in June of 1972 to provide services for the construction of the Mackenzie highway, and from this centre itinerant service has been provided by the department to the larger settlements, the frequency of visits depending on the need for services. With the slowdown if not the cessation of work on the highway in the course of 1972, since that time there has not been the same need for the department's services with respect to highway construction, but the department has remained close to the situation, and I can give the House the assurance that as needs develop, either with respect to the highway building program or to any other employment need or manpower training need in the Arctic, they will be met.
During 1972 a total of 17,337 workers and employer clients requested assistance. Of the clients seeking employment, 5,316 were placed. Workers were assisted under the Canada Manpower Mobility Program to travel to training institutions and to either explore or accept jobs away from their normal place of residence. Increased oil
January 10, 1974

exploration in the Mackenzie Delta and Arctic islands and the construction of the Mackenzie and Dempster highways provided employment for people who had limited previous exposure to a wage economy. Counselling services continue to be of prime importance because of the major development taking place and the special problems encountered by people from isolated areas who are on the threshold of a changing life style.
There have been substantial increases in the number of courses offered and greater participation in training for both the Yukon territory and the Northwest Territories. Courses geared to present and future economic needs of the developing economy are producing graduates trained as heavy equipment operators, pipeline equipment operators, underground miners, and clerk typists to name a few. Other special courses provided by the department include game guide, fire suppression, prospecting, arts and crafts, rod and chainmen and business management. An expanded Manpower Industrial Training Program resulted in significant use of the program, particularly in the mining and service industries. Courses and basic training for skill development and basic industrial skills were offered in more than 16 settlements during 1972. Basic literacy and life skills were added to basic education courses. First and second year apprenticeship courses in carpentry and heavy duty mechanics were offered for the first time in the Northwest Territories.
With respect to direct employment programs, we have of course made available to people in the north departmental programs through LIP, and now also through LEAP. For the 1973-74 year there have been 28 projects approved under the Local Initiatives Program for a total of $506,892. I expect that these programs are now in operation.
Vocational rehabilitation of disabled persons agreements are held between the department and the government of the Territories. The agreement's main function is to provide comprehensive rehabilitation services to disabled persons. Services include medical and manpower assessment, training and placement, and are achieved through co-operation with other agencies. I may mention that there is a small amount of immigration from other countries to the Northwest Territories and this also comes under the aegis of the department.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that the department is just as conscious of its responsibilities toward the people of the Northwest Territories as it is toward those in other parts of the country. As I stated earlier it is remaining in close touch with developments and will be prepared to meet any needs which may develop with all the resources it has available.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-REQUEST FOR COPY OF TRAINING AND EMPLOYMENT AGREEMENTS PREPARED BY INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since this topic has been the subject of two reports of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development,
I should like to remind the House of the gist of those reports and to reiterate what I consider to be an unsatisfactory situation as far as the employment of Indian people in Canada is concerned.
The rate of unemployment among Indian people in Canada remains in excess of 50 per cent. That is totally unacceptable. There are a number of solutions, but there is one in particular which I have pushed with ministers who have occupied that portfolio since 1964-65. I think the first time I made this representation was in 1964, when Jack Nicholson was minister. We have not tried the simple, obvious thing, and sometimes it seems to me that obvious steps are ignored by civil servants who appear to feel that more complicated steps are necessary to achieve a solution.
The obvious way to help the employment situation for Indian people in Canada is to bring together regionally, provincially or nationally-and I think regionally would make the most sense-the people who are most concerned with the problem. I mean the representatives of the companies involved in northern resource exploitation, the representatives of labour unions that might be involved, the representatives of course, of the Indian people involved as well as representatives of the federal and provincial governments. These people should be exposed to the success stories that have occurred across the north as far as the employment of Indian people is concerned. Some specific companies have shown a special understanding of the Indian people because they have had sympathetic foremen or personnel managers. These people appreciated the difficulties of individuals transferred from one form of making a living to another; they understood that sometimes there was need for an adjustment to rigid time schedules or rigid working hours which were not always acceptable or easily tolerated by the native people of the north. As a result, there have been what the companies consider failures of adjustment among Indian workers and this results in a lack of enthusiasm for hiring them.

January 10, 1974
Mackenzie Valley Pipeline
I am convinced that this situation could be overcome to a large extent if the people most concerned with employment in the north were exposed to the success stories that do exist. The suggestion was made to various ministers by letter and, finally, in 1969 the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development made certain recommendations. The committee report outlined the Indian job situation and made the following recommendations:
The committee urges that regional conferences be held, bringing together all the elements capable of solving the unemployment problem. These include representatives of federal and provincial departments and agencies directly concerned, organized labour, industries located in the general areas of high Indian and Eskimo unemployment and of the Indian and Eskimo people.
Such conferences would permit:
(a) the establishment of better lines of communication and co-ordination among all the parties involved;
'b) the exchange and sharing of information concerning successful employment programs involving Indian and Eskimo people and northern employers;
(c) underlining the crisis proportions of the Indian and Eskimo unemployment and under-employment problem.
The committee also urges the government to exercise more authority in the application of conditions relating to the hiring of northern residents contained in the Northern Minerals Assistance Program.
And so on. This committee report dated May 29, 1969, which is 4*/2 years ago, was followed by another report, the report on education of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Incidentally, both these committees' reports enjoyed the unanimous support of all parties in the House. This second report dated June 22, 1971, refers to the earlier report and says:
In its report to the House dated May 29, 1969, this committee urged the convocation of regional conferences including representatives of federal and provincial departments directly concerned, organized labour, industries located in the general areas of Indian and Eskimo unemployment, and of representatives of the Indian and Eskimo people, to permit, among other things, the exchange and sharing of information concerning successful employment programs involving Indian and Eskimo people and northern employers. The committee is very disappointed that the government failed to act upon this recommendation and notes as the committee predicted in 1969 that the unemployment problem among Canada's Indian and Eskimo peoples has, if anything, grown worse. Industrial attitudes, although improving, are improving too slowly. Since the government appears unwilling to act to convoke such regional conferences, the committee now suggests that the task of organizing and convening such regional conferences should be handed over to the appropriate regional Indian organizations and that the Government of Canada, through either the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development or the Department of Manpower, provide the necessary funding.
The committee is convinced that much greater use should be made by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in particular, and other government departments as well, of the willingness of provincial regional, and national Indian organizations, to collaborate with government in evolving vocational programs and employment programs attuned to the needs and skills of our Indian people and to the needs of industries located in the regions where our Indian people live and are available for work.
The report continues:
Vocational programs for Indian youth must not only be integrated with local industrial needs but should include on-job training as a major part of any vocational training course. In addition to the obvious benefits of improved practical training and increased employment opportunities which would flow from such an approach there would 
also be a useful pressure on vocational school programs to develop the types of training and courses needed by industry.
I do not intend to labour the point further. Two reports by standing committees of this House have urged action. The second report urges that if the government does not intend to do something, at least it should support Indian organizations which might be willing to act. I urge the National Indian Brotherhood to act on this recommendation. I also urge the government to support with funding any such initiative which the National Indian Brotherhood or any provincial Indian organization might take in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, this is another issue which may seem small as far as the amendment is concerned. We certainly will not detain the House on it. However, in pursuance of our duty to make this bill better and to take care of what we think are errors in drafting which could have serious consequences, I have moved the amendment.

January 10, 1974

I ask hon. members to look at clause 11. Even as it has now been amended by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) and by the amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), it still reads as follows; and this is the heart, the kernel, the pith and substance of the whole field:
When the governor in council is of the opinion that a national emergency exists by reason of actual or anticipated shortages of petroleum-
I stop there and ask hon. members to bear in mind the word "anticipated". Up to that point the governor in council can be of the opinion that a national emergency exists because it believes that some time in the future there will be shortages of petroleum. It further reads:
-or disturbances in the petroleum markets that affect or will affect-
I ask hon. members to use plain common sense and put those two thoughts together. Put together, they give to the governor in council the right to say that a national emergency exists in this country because there is an anticipated shortage; in other words, that some time in the future there is likely to be a shortage of petroleum products and that possibly may affect the national security. In the name of heaven, are we going to permit the governor in council, with those two vague possibilities, to declare that a national emergency exists? It is all very well to say that the governor in council is composed of reasonable men. That is true enough, they may be reasonable men; but even reasonable men panic. There may be other reasons for this provision in the bill, but I suggest to Your Honour that if the governor in council is to decide, we are likely to be entering upon a period of shortage-

Motion No. 3.
That Bill C-236, an act to provide a means to conserve the supplies of petroleum products within Canada during periods of national emergency caused by shortages or market disturbances affecting the national security and welfare and the economic stability of Canada, and to amend the National Energy Board Act, be amended in clause 11 thereof
Energy Supplies Emergency Act
by deleting the words "that affect of will affect" in lines 5 and 6 on page 6 and substituting the word "affecting".
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am glad to hear from the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis). I am reminded of an occasion when one of his former colleagues, Mr. Douglas Fisher, was dealing with a private member's public bill. He started on a long speech but found out two-thirds of the way through that he was dealing with another bill entirely, and we on these benches pointed it out to him. The hon. member for York South is just repaying the courtesy which was extended. If there are hon. members who have not been following me and who wish me to repeat what I have said, I shall be glad to do so, but if they remain silent I will proceed to draw their attention to motion No. 3 which deals with clause 11 as amended.
I think I can sum up by submission by saying it is asking too much of this House to give the governor in council the power to declare a national emergency where it is dependent upon the two events taking place, the possibility of which might be present but which in actuality do not exist. Let us interpret what might happen, in a common sense way. The governor in council could say, "We think that some time next month, because the international situation suggests to us that the war in the Middle East may be resumed, there is likely to be a shortage of fuel supplies leading to a national emergency." That is one element. The other element is the decision that this situation would affect the national security. I think it is too much to ask us to accept the right of the governor-in-council to put these two contingent events together.
I am reinforced in my view because the wording which I am striving for in my amendment is that which appears in the long title. It is the same wording that appears in the recommendation. The long title of Bill C-236 is as follows: An act to provide a means to conserve the supplies of petroleum products within Canada during periods of national emergency caused by shortages or market disturbances affecting the national security-
It does not use the words which the draftsman has used in this case as a result of the instructions he has received, and I am asking that we go back to what the title says. Similarly, in the recommendation the same language appears. It is:
His Excellency the Governor General has recommended to the House of Commons the present measure to provide a means to conserve the supplies of petroleum products in Canada during periods of national emergency caused by shortages or market disturbances affecting the national security-
And so on. All I am asking is that the House restore the wording in clause 11 to what was obviously in the minds of those who first conceived this act and was in the mind of the Governor General when he made the recommendation upon which the bill is founded.
I shall conclude on this note. As I mentioned yesterday afternoon when dealing with the first amendment, our party has no intention of challenging the passage of this bill because of its doubtful constitutional character. I might point out, though, that others might wish to do so at a later date should a national emergency be proclaimed.
The minister and I took part in an exchange of views the other day with regard to the position of the federal government under the federal system and the circumstances in which it may interfere with the rights enjoyed by the

January 10, 1974
Energy Supplies Emergency Act
provinces. We agree that such cases as the Fort Francis case have determined this issue for a great many years. The fact remains that irrespective of what the government may say-the government may say that there is an emergency every day of the week for two months-and even though this House, following acceptance of the amendment by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, might agree with the government in declaring there is an emergency which warrants the governor in council proclaiming one, this does not necessarily make it so. It remains a matter of fact to be determined by the circumstances.
If you apply the case I have cited to the situation with regard to petroleum products, I suggest strongly, as a member of the bar for a great many years, that any court would throw out a declaration of a national emergency based on the ground that there might be a shortage of petroleum products which could affect the national security at some time in the future. It is for this reason, and in an effort to be helpful to the minister, to try to improve the language of the bill which was in all likelihood put together hastily at the instance of the technical advisory committee, that I make these observations. I think the minister would be in a much better position if he would go back to the wording which appears in the long title and in the recommendation and make the slight substitution which I am proposing.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ALLOCATION BOARD, MANDATORY ALLOCATION OF SUPPLIES AND RATIONING OF CONTROLLED PRODUCTS

speechtext:
I should like to get back to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). This is really the kernel of the whole legislation, as clause 11 provides:
When the governor in council is of the opinion that a national emergency exists by reason of actual or anticipated shortages of petroleum or disturbances in the petroleum markets that affect or will affect the national security and welfare and the economic stability of Canada, and that it is necessary in the national interest to conserve the supplies of petroleum products within Canada, the governor in council may, by order, so declare-
This is a very important clause because it is the whole reason for introducing the legislation. I am somewhat disturbed by the remarks I heard from some members during the course of the discussion yesterday and today, to the effect that there is a phony sort of an emergency oil crisis in Canada. I noticed an article in tonight's Ottawa Citizen by Mr. Charles Lynch under the heading "The crisis that isn't". He quotes the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Bawden), who said that 5 per cent more crude oil has been distributed to eastern Canada this year than last year and therefore there is not any shortage. The hon. member also made some interjections yesterday to that effect.
Let me say, first of all, that I would be surprised if the supplies of crude oil delivered to refineries this year were not greater than last year, because for months every effort has been made to get western crude to eastern Canada, through the Seaway, around by the Panama Canal, by rail and by truck. Undoubtedly, much of this oil is being stockpiled in anticipation of the fact that it may not be possible to deliver adequate supplies in the winter months. Undoubtedly, the people in eastern Canada have been fortunate in that we have had a mild winter so far: the St. Lawrence Seaway stayed open much longer than usual and some 100,000 barrels a day were able to be shipped well into December. We are fortunate that the weather has been mild and there has not been the same demand for heating oil-but we are not out yet of the woods by any manner or means.
Let me point out that members in all parts of the House, particularly those who sit in the opposition parties, were pressing the government a few months ago to recognize the fact that there could be an oil shortage in eastern Canada, urging them to take the steps necessary to meet

January 10, 1974
Energy Supplies Emergency Act that anticipated oil shortage. If the shortage does not materialize, no one is going to suffer. But I can imagine what we would be saying on this side of the House if the government had not anticipated an oil shortage and had not taken some of the steps necessary to cope with it. Only time will tell whether the steps they have taken are adequate. Certainly steps had to be taken, and I am glad some steps have been taken. I hope they will obviate any hardship on the part of the people who live in eastern Canada.
It is a mistake to think that clause 11 is only going to be required for this winter. If the pipeline to Montreal is not completed until 1976-and I certainly feel, after the statement by the minister, that it will probably be mid-summer of this year before construction starts; it is more likely to be 1976 than 1975-then we have two more winters during which the people of eastern Canada will be largely dependent upon offshore oil. That oil may be very difficult to procure because there are still the problems of restrictions, embargoes and diversions.
It is rather significant that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) said that the government of Saudi Arabia has indicated that we can have the oil we want, but we are not getting any. The very evident reason for that is that the oil which the government of Saudi Arabia is willing to send to Canada is being diverted elsewhere somewhere along the line by the companies which purchase that oil. It is comparatively easy to divert oil in mid-ocean and send it to some destination other than the one put on the bill of lading.
So the possibility-and all of us hope it will not materialize-of serious oil shortages in eastern Canada until such time as the pipeline is built is a fact which this House of Commons has to consider seriously and we have to give the government the necessary powers to deal with such an emergency should it arise. I commend my friends in the Conservative Party for having proposed an amendment in order to give the House of Commons the right to declare whether or not they agree with the government that there is an emergency. We now have the provision in the bill by which the government must come back to parliament to get the House of Commons to declare that there is such an emergency.
The amendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) would change clause 11 so that it would read:
When the governor in council is of the opinion that a national emergency exists by reason of actual or anticipated shortages of petroleum or disturbances in the petroleum markets affecting the national security-
As my colleague, the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) pointed out, if you strike out "will affect" you ought also to strike out "anticipated". It is not possible to talk about an anticipated shortage which affects you now; it can only be an anticipated shortage which will affect you when the shortage takes place. Since the art of governing is the art of foreseeing, it may be necessary for the government to set up an energy allocation board to allocate certain supplies of oil and to provide for storage of oil in certain areas of Canada in anticipation of something which does not affect Canada at the time but which will affect it in the future.

Therefore, it seems to me that not only from a grammatical standpoint but in terms of logic and, although I am not a lawyer, I would think in terms of law, if you are going to deal with an actual shortage then you deal with a shortage which affects us now; and if you are also going to give the government power to deal with an anticipated shortage, you must give it power to deal with something which will affect Canada at some future time but which does not affect Canada at the present time. For that reason, it seems to me that the amendment is unwise and that the present provisions in clause 11 ought to stand.

That Bill C-236, An Act to provide a means to conserve the supplies of petroleum products within Canada during periods of national emergency caused by shortages or market disturbances affecting the national security and welfare and the economic stability of Canada, and to amend the National Energy Board Act, be amended by deleting subclause 12(5), lines 17 to 23 on page 7, and renumbering the subsequent sub-clause accordingly.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ALLOCATION BOARD, MANDATORY ALLOCATION OF SUPPLIES AND RATIONING OF CONTROLLED PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reason for moving this amendment is that it is just one more small attempt on our part to improve what is really a terrible bill and a very poor way in which to attempt to solve a potential problem about which the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) spoke about a moment ago. The mentality of the Liberal and NDP members in their approach to the question of a potential shortfall in energy and their approach to this bill could be exemplied, I think, by the remarks the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais) made yesterday afternoon, as recorded at page 9219 of Hansard, when he criticized our party by saying we were attempting to delay this bill. He stated:
-I recognized the seriousness of the emergency we were facing, and the potential emergency for which the government was attempting to prepare. We had but to read the newspapers to be convinced of the fact that we were facing very serious difficulties indeed.
What a ludicrous statement! The minister comes into this House one day and says we could be short 75,000 barrels of oil, and a few days later that we could be short 200,000 barrels of oil a day. The hon. member for Nipissing reads the newspapers reporting the minister's statement and decides we must be facing an oil crisis. They panic just like Chicken Little in the children's story: The sky is falling in! The turkey-lurkeys in the NDP say, "Yes, it is; we must do something". So the government produces this bill which asks for enormous powers. Basically, it asks that the minister be able unilaterally to declare a national emergency and take over the distribution of almost everything in this country.
In this party we recognize that indeed there is a potential short supply of oil in the eastern part of this country. We recognized this possibility many years ago and recommended then that a pipeline be built to Montreal. Mr. Speaker, if you read the same newspapers as the hon. member for Nipissing, you will recall that there was a Middle East war in 1967 and that a lasting peace did not develop. It should have been realized that a disruption in respect of petroleum existed from 1967, and at least some preparation at that time would have been the act of a prudent government.
It is obvious that no such precautions were taken and that no contingency plan existed. It is obvious, also, that very quickly draftsmen sat down and produced this bill. One example of the excessive power demanded by this bill is clause 12 (5) which this amendment would seek to delete. This clause provides:
The governor in council may, by order, add any product that is manufactured wholly or in part from petroleum to the mandatory allocation program and thereupon that product becomes a controlled product for the purpose of the allocation of the supplies thereof in Canada.
Energy Supplies Emergency Act
That clause would give this board the power to allocate, and ultimately ration, almost every product related in any way, shape or form to petroleum which is an important feedstock and base for so many things. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding) talked about nylon stockings. Indeed the government could allocate these- and garbage bags, toothbrushes, roofing tile, telephones, rubber tires, rubber balloons and other rubber products. This is the granting of far too much power to any board, let alone a board under the direction of this particular minister whose credibility is at least to be questioned.
I would think that every member of this House, when he read this clause, must have raised his eyebrows. Certainly we did. However, we permitted the bill to go to the committee in the hope that in committee we would be able to call sufficient witnesses to determine whether in fact there is a potential crisis, how much the shortfall might be this winter and how much other products might be affected by the shortfall. We wanted to examine this legislation carefully, but we were obstructed at every opportunity. My colleague the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) yesterday alluded to this fact.
The hon. member for Nipissing indicated by his behaviour in the committee that it was the government's intention not to allow us to call the necessary witnesses and obtain some facts and information in order to judge this bill in the proper context, with proper information and not just on the emotional situations which the minister, I suggest, has possibly created deliberately to indicate that there is an atmosphere of crisis ahead. However, we did obtain some information; we did hear some witnesses. Mr. Stabback, who was not allowed to appear alone, appeared as the minister's adviser. He did answer some questions directly, however. In answer to a question put to him by the hon. member for Kootenay West, he said:
I think the difficulties that are facing the plastic industry, Mr. Harding, are related to the shortfall in ethylene supplies that became apparent before the present emergency in North America. As you know, the Canadian industry is endeavouring to establish new ethylene plants in Canada as their response towards meeting the shortfall. We have been made aware by some companies of their difficulty in obtaining raw material for their processing.
The point is that this shortfall in ethylene was apparent to the National Energy Board before there was any concern about crude oil. The hon. member for York North (Mr. Danson) asked a question of Mr. Stabback in the committee. He said:
If I understand Mr. Stabback correctly, the interpretation is that the current shortage of, perhaps, crude and gas is not the reason for the shortfall in petrochemical products in so far as the plastics industry is concerned. It is one of downstream capacity in refining. Is that not correct?
This is from a Liberal member. Mr. Stabback replied:
It is not the primary reason. Of course, it exacerbates it, but it was really related to a shortfall in the supply of ethylene emanating from United States plants and resulting from, amongst other things, a reduction in supplies of natural gas that are now available in the southern part of the United States.
In other words, the shortfall in respect of plastics alluded to by the hon. member for Kootenay West and the hon. member for York North were not related to any shortfall of crude oil from the Middle East area but were related to shortfalls in plant capacity which were in existence long before this bill was presented. It would seem very reason-

January 10, 1974
Energy Supplies Emergency Act
able, if shortages of this type were not caused by energy allocation problems, that we should not use the energy allocation board to try to solve these problems.
My colleague, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) asked the minister some questions in the committee. He recognized that some petrochemicals could be in short supply as a result of this energy crisis, but suggested these are fairly limited in scope. He asked the minister if he would be willing to tighten up the wording of this clause, and the minister replied no: He said:
I think it is conceivable that if there was a grievous shortage of these things in Canada it might be desirable to take this jurisdiction.
I pursued this question along similar lines, and the minister replied in respect of agricultural chemicals, which are in short supply, as you may be aware, Mr. Speaker, not as a result of the crude oil shortage but, rather, as a result of lack of plant capacity. He said:
-you take an agricultural chemical that may be dependent upon a petroleum derivative and saying that the government should not be in a position to allocate short supplies there, even though that may be as much of a detriment at increasing food production as not having tractor fuel available ... It seems to me that it is reasonable to extend the jurisdiction here to protect the public as much in that situation as in the case of fuel.
Again I explained in committee what is common knowledge to people cognizant of the industry, that the problem of the shortfall in agricultural chemicals and petrochemicals is the result of lack of plant capacity. If you want to put the blame, go back to federal fiscal and financial policies, to the policies of the predecessor of the present Minister of Finance-the man of the year, the Hon. Edgar Benson. These problems were caused by the fiscal and financial policies of this government, and it would seem to me quite reasonable to think that is the way in which a solution should be sought. I raised this point with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), who said:
Well, it seems to me in principle it is the same problem.
That explains the reason for moving this amendment. Had, in fact, the government taken the position that the points raised by Mr. Stabback were valid, namely, that this allocation board should be in a position to tell refiners what to do with the effluent from refineries, ethylene, benzene and other aromatics, which might go into petrochemical production, I would have agreed. But when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources states that this energy allocation board might allocate any product that is in short supply and is related to petroleum for no matter what reason, that is overstepping the bounds.
The second reason for moving our motion is that this bill is an excuse for inaction. There are grievous problems in this country with respect to agricultural chemicals. Some farmers are not able to get fertilizer, and this could have serious consequences on their production and on food prices in Canada. Many manufacturing concerns are having difficulty in finding plastic feedstock which they need to manufacture toothbrushes and a number of other products. These are very important problems to which this government has not addressed itself in any noticeable way. They are the responsibility of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray), the Minister of

Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) since it is the fiscal and financial policies of this government in the past which have caused these grievous shortages at this time. So there are two reasons. The first is that the powers asked by the minister in this clause go far beyond anything which one would call reasonable.
At this point it might be worth mentioning the make-up of the Energy Board. It will consist of a chairman drawn from the public service who is knowledgeable in this area, a nominee from the province of Quebec as a consuming province, a nominee from the province of Alberta as a producing province, a nominee from industry or somebody seconded from industry who is knowledgeable in marketing, and someone who is knowledgeable in the consumption end of fuels, as suggested by the minister. None of these people has any expertise in the area of plastics, the area of consumer products related to plastics, and it would be most inappropriate to give these powers to the board because I am sure they will cause ten times the number of problems as they will attempt to cure.
The second reason is as follows. We have seen what this government has done with the Food Prices Review Board. They have used it as an excuse for doing nothing about the price of food in Canada. To give this energy resources board potential responsibility for all the shortages in plastics, agricultural and other chemicals, would give them just another excuse for continued inaction in the areas of fiscal, financial policy and trade.
However, the main and the third reason for moving this motion is that the government already has the power under this bill to control all the products which are the base or the feedstock of the petrochemical industry, because in clause 2 under the definition of "petroleum products" we find the following:
"petroleum" or "petroleum product" means crude oil or other hydrocarbon or mixture of hydrocarbons recovered in liquid or solid state from a natural reservoir, any hydrocarbon or mixture thereof, in liquid or solid state, that results from the processing or refining of crude oil or other hydrocarbon,
It goes on to include natural gasoline and natural gas. That includes all the chemical feedstocks. It includes ethylene, which Mr. Stabback, vice-chairman of the National Energy Board, talked about being potentially in short supply. It is a refinery product, or is manufactured from ethane which is a product of a gas processing plant. Benzene, phenol and other aromatic compounds which are products of refineries and are important chemical-building stocks, according to this definition fall within the realm of petroleum and petroleum products. Therefore, this board is perfectly capable of looking after the allocation of these products.
Under other parts of this bill, in view of the generous definition of petroleum and petroleum products-and I have no argument about that; it is an appropriate definition-the minister can look after any shortfalls in plastics or petroleum-related products, agricultural chemicals, and so on, which have anything to do with a crude oil shortage. This bill would allow him to get into the business of allocating fertilizers, toothbrushes, and so on, even though they may have nothing to do with the shortage of crude oil but may be related to shortfalls in plant capacity or, presumably, a strike if there were a strike in a plastics
January 10, 1974

plant that would create shortfalls of plastics. The government could get into the act, according to the bill.
The scope is far too wide. Also, judging from the record of this minister, in particular in handling the energy situation, and the totally inaccurate information he has given the House repeatedly and in statements made to people outside the House, it would be inappropriate to trust him with that sort of authority. It would be dangerous to the people affected to give the government an excuse for inaction in these areas where there are very serious problems. I wonder why the government has not sought to take some action to clear up these problems which are causing people to lose their jobs.
Under the act as it exists, under the definition of petroleum and petroleum products in clause 2, this board would have the authority to look after the allocation of all petrochemical feedstocks to all petrochemical processing plants within Canada. Therefore, 1 would hope that the other members of this House would agree with me that in the interests of improving the bill we should strike out this clause.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ALLOCATION BOARD, MANDATORY ALLOCATION OF SUPPLIES AND RATIONING OF CONTROLLED PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of my colleagues has suggested that we would have done better with the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). I am looking at the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Peace River which we opposed in committee. We see no reason to change our minds this evening. The amendment offered by the Conservative Party will make the allocation program much less effective than we feel it should be. I should like to point out that the allocation board is going to be made up of responsible citizens. Different viewpoints will certainly be represented on the board, and when a decision is made by the board it must come to the governor in council-the cabinet-and it will be responsible for any controls that are imposed. I think it will be careful of the type of allocation program that goes into effect.
Let us look at the section which the hon. member wants to wipe out entirely. This is how clause 12(5) reads:
The governor in council may, by order, add any product that is manufactured wholly or in part from petroleum to the mandatory allocation program and thereupon that product becomes a controlled product for the purpose of the allocation of the supplies thereof in Canada.
I can think of a number of products that might be added to a program such as this. One of them is rosin. In British Columbia, several industries have already indicated that because of the shortage of rosin they will either have to close down or curtail employment. If the allocation of supplies is needed to keep up the supply of rosin, or if rosin is in short supply, then it seems logical to me that this product should be brought under the control of the allocation board which can see to it that these industries keep working. There are a host of other circumstances where similar logic could apply, and that is why I believe this clause must be retained. The board will not be hard on any specific industry and I am quite certain that it will not abuse the allocation of supplies.
It seems to me, for example, that there might be a need to stop some of the crude oil going to the petrochemical
Energy Supplies Emergency Act industry, or in some cases to allocate additional supplies of crude oil to that industry if certain products are needed. That is the value of having this provision, but the Tories are out to weaken the bill as much as possible so the program will not work.
We have heard about plastic cups and other plastic materials, Mr. Speaker. If we get into an emergency situation, the allocation board may have to decide where the priority lies. The whole field of oil products comes into this picture. If we have an extreme situation where we need a great deal of heating oil, for example, we will have to divert more crude petroleum into the refineries which are going to produce it. This might force us to stop supplies of crude oil going to some other branches of the petrochemical industry where plastics and other products are made. It is as simple as that. In an emergency, I think the board must have control and be able to tell the oil companies and the people of Canada where the crude oil should go and where oil products should go if they have to be rationed.
We in this party feel that this clause will help in a crisis and we have no hesitation in asking the House to turn down the amendment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) spoke about this question. In the depth of his compassion he has now left the House, which I regret. There are three points to be made with regard to his particular observation. The first is his reference to fiscal provisions in the past which had inhibited the Canadian petrochemical industry. As anyone would know who has reflected for any particular period of time on the Canadian petrochemical industry, the problem has been one of scale and particularly of access to the United States

January 10, 1974
Energy Supplies Emergency Act
market by Canadian firms. Of course, this has not been a question of Canadian fiscal policy, but a question of international negotiations within the ambit of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. Basically, the question is whether the Canadian industry has been able to gain favourable access to the United States market, which in fact they have not been able to do over a period of time.
Secondly, if this is so, then who is to provide, on an economic scale, for the needs of Canadian industry and the Canadian consumer community in this particular area of product? There has been a whole range of products; some have come from Canadian sources but the great majority come from overseas. We talk at length with regard to the importation of butadiene from Polysar which, because of sources in Canada, necessarily had to come from abroad. There is a whole range of Canadian products, some of which are dependent upon United States sources. If there is a general shortening of international supply in these particular products, inevitably it is going to affect Canada. Whether one allocates it or not, if there is a shortage of supply in the feedstocks of these particular commodities in their chemical derivations, the fact is that the Canadian community will have to run short.
The hon. member spoke in rather disparaging fashion about a whole range of consumer products which are of importance to Canadians. He suggested that they will run short of these things. Basically, his position and that of his party is: Well, let them run short.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question or privilege. If I may speak under the Standing Order which the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) cited last night, to do with memberk opposite putting words into one's mouth, I wish to state that at no time did I or anybody in this party suggest that these potential and existing shortages of rosin, butadiene, ethylene and other chemicals are not serious. They are very serious. Indeed, I made the point of wondering out loud why the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie), who has responsibility in this area, has not done anything to date. People are suffering in British Columbia, Ontario, Alberta, and indeed in every part of the country.
If the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) would turn around one day and talk to his colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and ask why he does not get on with the job, he would be doing much more for the country than he is in proposing this clause in this bill at this time.

The difference between the approach of the hon. member for Calgary Centre and my approach to consumers in Canada who are threatened by this shortcoming is this: I wonder whether we should not express some concern and do something about the shortcoming, and he wants to brush it aside on a legality.
This bill would permit the government of Canada and the energy allocation board to take action and try to

protect Canadian consumers against this kind of shortfall. But the hon. member for Calgary Centre is not asking the House to do anything. He opposes, basically, this one power that we can adopt under this statute which is necessary for protecting Canadian consumers with regard to the whole range of products which he has mentioned and which I regard as being important. He and his colleagues referred in disparaging fashion to a whole group of consumer products as though people are not important.
